content.text:
Found it: **[ENT-1451 — Limit checkpoint branch sync to one remote](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1451/limit-checkpoint-branch-sync-to-one-remote)**, created today by Rizèl Scarlett from Slack feedback (an Insider named rizel). It's in Backlog on the Entire team, project `entire-cli`, no priority or assignee yet.

## What the ticket asks

With multiple remotes (e.g. `origin` and `publish`), **any** `git push` to **either** remote also syncs the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch to that remote — so checkpoint transcripts end up on `publish`, where the reporter doesn't want them. They know about `checkpoint_remote` but find it too GitHub-coupled, and propose a zero-config default: **only sync checkpoints to the first remote added**.

## How the code actually behaves today

The report matches the implementation. Git's pre-push hook passes the remote name as `$1`, and the strategy faithfully follows it — `PrePush(ctx, remote)` in `cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_push.go:40` resolves push settings per-remote (`resolvePushSettings(ctx, remote)`) and pushes checkpoint data to whatever remote the user happened to push. There's no notion of a "canonical checkpoint remote" unless you configure `checkpoint_remote` explicitly.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The behavior actually **differs by checkpoint backend**: with the git-branch primary, every push re-syncs the full `v1` branch, so both remotes get transcripts (this ticket). With the git-refs primary, the flock-JSONL push queue is drained by the *first* successful push, so the *second* remote silently gets nothing — the mirror-image bug, already filed as **ENCLI-256**.
- "First remote added" is trickier than it sounds: git doesn't store remote creation order anywhere reliable. The practical proxies are `origin` (git's conventional default), `checkout.defaultRemoteName`, or the remote the branch's upstream tracks — a fix would need to pick one and pin it in repo state rather than re-guessing.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## Related existing tickets worth linking

This sits in a small cluster of multi-remote issues that ENT-1451 doesn't currently reference:

- **ENCLI-255** (Triage) — reads/fetches hardcode `origin` while pushes follow the hook remote, so non-origin setups are already half-broken in the other direction.
- **ENCLI-256** (Triage) — the git-refs push-queue drain bug described above.
- **ENCLI-132** (Done) — the original `checkpoint_remote` feature request the reporter mentions.
- **ENCLI-53 / ENCLI-74** — the broader privacy concern (transcripts inheriting the repo's access model) that motivates not wanting checkpoints on a public `publish` remote.

A sensible fix shape would be: record the checkpoint sync remote once (defaulting to `origin`, or the sole remote if there's only one) in repo-local state, have `prePush` no-op when `$1` doesn't match it, and offer a lightweight `strategy_options` override that's just a remote *name* — decoupled from the GitHub-provider `checkpoint_remote` config. That would also give ENCLI-255/256 a single canonical remote to route reads and the refs queue through.

Here's the full picture: **no fix PRs exist for either issue** — what exists is a stacked test-coverage series by soph that deliberately pins today's broken multi-remote behavior, waiting on exactly the decision ENT-1451 now forces.

## The PR landscape

| PR | State | What it carries |
|---|---|---|
| [#1636](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1636) (1/4) | **Merged** | The test plan (`docs/testing/git-remote-test-plan.md`), backend matrix, real-hook push infra |
| [#1637](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1637) (2/4) | Open, review required, idle since Jul 6 | Real-hook P0 tests, cross-machine fetch, an explain fix |
| [#1638](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1638) (3/4) | Open, stacked on #1637 | **`refs_queue_semantics_test.go`** — including `TestGitRefsQueue_TwoRemotesQueueClearedByFirstPush`, which pins the ENCLI-256 bug with a comment saying "flip this assertion when fixed" |
| [#1639](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1639) (4/4) | Open, stacked on #1638 | OPF pre-push, degraded remotes, shallow/partial clones, e2e |

Both GitHub issues (#1634, #1635) are open with zero comments — nobody has started a fix.

## The connective tissue: decision D-1

The merged test plan on main already names the blocker at `docs/testing/git-remote-test-plan.md:148` — **decision D-1**: "pushing checkpoints to `upstream` (hook `$1`) while every read path fetches from `origin` is incoherent. Decide: teach reads to use the checkpoint-bearing remote… or document origin-only support and warn on non-origin pushes." The plan's PR 4 (the B1–B7 multi-remote tests: upstream-only repos, fork triangles, tracking-config divergence) is explicitly deferred until D-1 is decided — and those tests were **never written**; the open series stops short of them.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- ENT-1451 isn't just "related" to ENCLI-255/256 — it's the **user-facing forcing function for D-1**. Rizel's ask ("sync to one remote, zero config") is a concrete answer to the open decision: pick a single canonical checkpoint remote, route both pushes *and* reads through it. One decision resolves all three tickets.
- The stacked-PR structure matters for sequencing: #1638's queue-semantics test pins ENCLI-256's current behavior, so a fix should either land *after* the series merges (flipping the pinned assertion, as the test's comment instructs) or absorb that test file directly — otherwise the fix and the pin race each other.
- Note the asymmetry the fix must handle: git-branch backend **over-shares** (every remote gets `v1`), git-refs backend **under-shares** (first push drains the queue, second remote gets nothing). A "canonical checkpoint remote" concept fixes both with the same predicate: `remote == checkpointRemote ? sync : skip`.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## Suggested sequencing

1. Decide D-1 as "single canonical checkpoint remote" (ENT-1451's proposal, defaulting to `origin` / the sole remote).
2. Revive or merge the #1637–#1639 stack first (it's been idle ~3.5 weeks and #1637 needs review) so the pin tests exist to flip.
3. Implement the fix: gate `prePush` on the canonical remote (fixes ENT-1451 and ENCLI-256's option 2), point the hardcoded-origin read paths at the same resolver (ENCLI-255), then write the deferred B1–B7 tests against the now-defined behavior.

Want me to draft the D-1 decision + fix scoping as a comment on ENT-1451, or link the three tickets together in Linear first?
so is the stacked PR basically likeguard against what hte new ticket wants but doesn't actually allow wht the ticket wants? 1636 was merged from stack

Yes, exactly. The stack is pure test coverage — zero behavior changes to push/read logic. It's what's called "characterization" or "pin" testing: assert what the code *does today*, even where today's behavior is known-broken, so that the codebase's actual behavior is documented executable-y and any future fix has to consciously flip an assertion rather than silently change semantics.

So relative to ENT-1451:

- **It doesn't allow what the ticket wants.** Nothing in #1636–#1639 stops checkpoints from syncing to `publish`, or makes reads follow a non-origin remote. After all four merge, the behavior Rizel complained about is unchanged — it's just *tested*.
- **It's not a guard *against* the ticket either** — it's scaffolding *for* it. The pins are written expecting to be flipped: `TestGitRefsQueue_TwoRemotesQueueClearedByFirstPush` in #1638 literally carries a comment saying to invert the assertion when the bug is fixed, and the plan's B4 test is specced as "pin that checkpoint reads still target origin" pending decision D-1.
- **What merged (#1636) is the least behavior-adjacent part**: the test plan document, the backend test matrix, real-hook push infrastructure, and hermeticity fixes. The multi-remote pins themselves are still sitting in the open stack.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Pin tests are how you make a known bug *safe to fix*: without them, a fix PR changes behavior nobody was asserting, and review can't distinguish "intended semantic change" from "accidental regression". With them, the fix's diff shows the flipped assertion right next to the code change.
- The stack's author (soph) deliberately stopped before the B1–B7 tests because those can't be written as pins-to-flip — they'd pin whichever D-1 answer gets chosen, and D-1 was undecided. ENT-1451 arriving is effectively the product signal that decides D-1.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

The practical upshot: implementing ENT-1451 doesn't conflict with the stack, but the ideal order is stack first (so the pins exist), fix second (flipping them), B1–B7 third (locking in the new single-remote semantics). If the stack stays stalled, the fix PR can also just absorb the relevant test files from #1638 and write them pre-flipped.

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by understanding the current project context, then ask questions one at a time to refine the idea. Once you understand what you're building, present the design and get user approval.

<HARD-GATE>
Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any project, or take any implementation action until you have presented a design and the user has approved it. This applies to EVERY project regardless of perceived simplicity.
</HARD-GATE>

## Anti-Pattern: "This Is Too Simple To Need A Design"

Every project goes through this process. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config change — all of them. "Simple" projects are where unexamined assumptions cause the most wasted work. The design can be short (a few sentences for truly simple projects), but you MUST present it and get approval.

## Checklist

You MUST create a task for each of these items and complete them in order:

1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer visual companion** (if topic will involve visual questions) — this is its own message, not combined with a clarifying question. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec review loop** — dispatch spec-document-reviewer subagent with precisely crafted review context (never your session history); fix issues and re-dispatch until approved (max 5 iterations, then surface to human)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## Process Flow

```dot
digraph brainstorming {
    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
    "Visual questions ahead?" [shape=diamond];
    "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions" [shape=box];
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" [shape=box];
    "Present design sections" [shape=box];
    "User approves design?" [shape=diamond];
    "Write design doc" [shape=box];
    "Spec review loop" [shape=box];
    "Spec review passed?" [shape=diamond];
    "User reviews spec?" [shape=diamond];
    "Invoke writing-plans skill" [shape=doublecircle];

    "Explore project context" -> "Visual questions ahead?";
    "Visual questions ahead?" -> "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" [label="yes"];
    "Visual questions ahead?" -> "Ask clarifying questions" [label="no"];
    "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
    "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" -> "Present design sections";
    "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";
    "User approves design?" -> "Present design sections" [label="no, revise"];
    "User approves design?" -> "Write design doc" [label="yes"];
    "Write design doc" -> "Spec review loop";
    "Spec review loop" -> "Spec review passed?";
    "Spec review passed?" -> "Spec review loop" [label="issues found,\nfix and re-dispatch"];
    "Spec review passed?" -> "User reviews spec?" [label="approved"];
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Write design doc" [label="changes requested"];
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Invoke writing-plans skill" [label="approved"];
}
```

**The terminal state is invoking writing-plans.** Do NOT invoke frontend-design, mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. The ONLY skill you invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans.

## The Process

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

## After the Design

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Review Loop:**
After writing the spec document:

1. Dispatch spec-document-reviewer subagent (see spec-document-reviewer-prompt.md)
2. If Issues Found: fix, re-dispatch, repeat until Approved
3. If loop exceeds 5 iterations, surface to human for guidance

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Key Principles

- **One question at a time** - Don't overwhelm with multiple questions
- **Multiple choice preferred** - Easier to answer than open-ended when possible
- **YAGNI ruthlessly** - Remove unnecessary features from all designs
- **Explore alternatives** - Always propose 2-3 approaches before settling
- **Incremental validation** - Present design, get approval before moving on
- **Be flexible** - Go back and clarify when something doesn't make sense

## Visual Companion

A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.

**Offering the companion:** When you anticipate that upcoming questions will involve visual content (mockups, layouts, diagrams), offer it once for consent:
> "Some of what we're working on might be easier to explain if I can show it to you in a web browser. I can put together mockups, diagrams, comparisons, and other visuals as we go. This feature is still new and can be token-intensive. Want to try it? (Requires opening a local URL)"

**This offer MUST be its own message.** Do not combine it with clarifying questions, context summaries, or any other content. The message should contain ONLY the offer above and nothing else. Wait for the user's response before continuing. If they decline, proceed with text-only brainstorming.

**Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**

- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions

A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.

If they agree to the companion, read the detailed guide before proceeding:
`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`

questions.question: Which scope should the ENT-1451 implementation target?

options.label: A: Push gate only (Recommended)
options.description: Canonical-remote resolver + prePush gate + config override. Fixes ENT-1451 and ENCLI-256; leaves read paths (ENCLI-255) for a follow-up. Small, safe diff.

options.label: B: Push gate + read paths
options.description: Everything in A, plus route the origin-hardcoded read/fetch paths through the same resolver, closing ENCLI-255 too. Bigger diff touching resume/explain/fetch code.

options.label: C: Config knob only
options.description: Add checkpoint_push_remote setting with no default gating. No behavior change unless configured — doesn't fully satisfy the zero-config ask.

content.text:
Happy to go deeper on A. Here's the full design.

## Approach A in detail

### 1. The resolver — one new function, one new setting

A new `resolveCheckpointSyncRemote(ctx) string` (living in the `strategy` package next to `resolvePushSettings`, or in `checkpoint/remote` if reads later want it — I'd start in `strategy` and only promote it when B happens). Resolution order:

1. **`strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote`** from settings — a plain remote name like `"origin"` or `"private"`. This is deliberately *not* the existing `checkpoint_remote` (which is a `{provider, repo}` struct that derives a whole separate URL and does fork detection). This is just "which of my existing remotes carries checkpoints."
2. **`origin`**, if `git remote get-url origin` succeeds.
3. **The sole remote**, if `git remote` lists exactly one.
4. **First remote in config order** — `git remote` outputs alphabetically, so this would read the first `[remote "…"]` section via `git config --get-regexp '^remote\..*\.url$'`, which preserves file order. This is the "first remote I added" case for origin-less, multi-remote repos.

Steps 2–4 mean zero configuration for ~everyone: a normal clone has `origin` and behaves exactly as today.

### 2. The gate — one early return in `prePush`

In `manual_commit_push.go`, right after `resolvePushSettings` (around `manual_commit_push.go:71`):

- If a dedicated `checkpoint_remote` URL resolved (`ps.hasCheckpointURL()`), **skip the gate** — checkpoints go to a dedicated store regardless of which remote triggered the push, which is today's documented behavior for that feature and shouldn't regress.
- Otherwise, if the hook's remote (`$1`, i.e. `ps.remote`) ≠ canonical remote → log a debug line ("checkpoint sync skipped: remote X is not the checkpoint remote Y") and `return nil`. The user's push proceeds untouched; no checkpoint refs, no v1 branch, no OPF prompt, no policy sync side effects on that remote.

Because the gate sits *before* both backend branches (git-refs at line 84, git-branch below), it covers both:

- **git-branch:** `publish` never receives `entire/checkpoints/v1`. That's ENT-1451 verbatim.
- **git-refs:** the push queue is only ever drained when pushing the canonical remote — `git push publish` no longer consumes queue entries, so a later `git push origin` still finds and pushes them. That's ENCLI-256's option 2, for free.

One subtlety: git passes a **URL** as `$1` when you `git push <url>` directly (no configured remote). URL-pushes won't match the canonical remote name and thus skip checkpoint sync — which I'd argue is correct (an ad-hoc URL push is even less "the checkpoint home" than a second remote), but it is a behavior change from today and gets a pin test.

### 3. What deliberately doesn't change

- Read/fetch paths stay hardcoded to `origin`. In the default resolution (`origin` wins), writes and reads now agree, so the common case is coherent. The incoherent leftover — someone sets `checkpoint_push_remote: "private"` and reads still look at `origin` — is exactly the ENCLI-255 follow-up (scope B), and the resolver is built so B can reuse it.
- `checkpoint_remote` (GitHub-coupled) keeps working unchanged.
- `push_sessions: false` still disables everything, checked before the gate as now.

### 4. Testing

- **Unit** (`strategy` package): resolver precedence table — override set / origin exists / sole remote / origin-less multi-remote / no remotes.
- **Integration** (`cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/`, per the CLAUDE.md isolated-temp-repo rules): two local bare remotes `origin` + `publish`; for **both backends**: push to `publish` → no checkpoint refs/v1 there, queue intact; then push to `origin` → checkpoints land, queue drained. Plus the `checkpoint_push_remote` override variant and the URL-push pin.
- **Collision watch:** #1638's `TestGitRefsQueue_TwoRemotesQueueClearedByFirstPush` pins the old behavior. If the stack merges first, this PR flips that assertion (as its comment instructs); if not, this PR adds its own equivalent test and the stack rebases.
- Standard gate: `mise run check` before commit.

### 5. Risks / edge cases considered

- **Fork triangles** (origin = my fork, upstream = base): checkpoints go to origin only — an improvement over today, where `git push upstream` would leak transcripts to the base repo.
- **Someone depends on multi-remote checkpoint sync** (e.g. a backup remote): they lose it silently. Mitigation: the debug log line, a changelog entry, and the knob as the escape hatch (though the knob picks *one* remote — true multi-remote sync becomes explicitly unsupported).
- **Remote renamed/deleted after override set:** resolver falls through? No — an explicitly configured name that doesn't exist should warn and *skip sync* rather than silently fall back to origin (fail-closed keeps private data private).

Rough size: ~1 new file (resolver + tests), ~15-line change in `manual_commit_push.go`, a settings field in `settings/settings.go`, integration tests. One PR, 2–3 commits.

Does this scope and shape look right to you — and in particular, do you agree with fail-closed on a misconfigured `checkpoint_push_remote`, and with skipping checkpoint sync on direct URL-pushes?
so you're saying that the resolver will limit the sync to one remote when multiple exist?

Almost — small but important distinction: the resolver just **answers a question** ("which one remote is the checkpoint home?"); the **gate in `prePush` is what actually limits the sync**. They work as a pair:

1. Every `git push <remote>` fires the pre-push hook, and git tells us which remote via `$1`. Today, checkpoint sync runs unconditionally — so with `origin` and `publish`, whichever one you push gets checkpoints. That's the bug.

2. Under the new design, each hook invocation calls the resolver, which returns exactly one name (say `origin` — via the override, or the origin-default, or sole-remote, or first-in-config fallback). It doesn't touch the network or push anything; it's a pure "who is canonical?" lookup.

3. The gate then compares: is *this* push going to the canonical remote?
   - `git push origin` → match → checkpoint sync runs exactly as today.
   - `git push publish` → no match → early return; the push proceeds as a completely ordinary git push, with no checkpoint branch, no per-checkpoint refs, no queue drain, no OPF prompt.

So the limiting happens by **skipping sync on every non-canonical push**, not by the resolver blocking anything itself. Checkpoint data ends up on exactly one remote no matter how many remotes exist or in what order you push them.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- This shape is forced by git's hook model: the pre-push hook runs once per push and only knows about *that* push's remote. You can't "push checkpoints to origin" from inside a `git push publish` hook without surprising side effects (pushing to a remote the user didn't name). So the only clean semantics are: act when the push targets the canonical remote, stay silent otherwise.
- It's also why the git-refs queue bug (ENCLI-256) vanishes: the queue was being consumed by whichever push came first. Once only canonical-remote pushes can touch the queue, "drained by the wrong remote" is unrepresentable.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

The one trade-off worth restating: if you *never* push the canonical remote, checkpoints accumulate locally and sync nowhere — same as today when you never push at all, but now also true if you exclusively push `publish`. That's inherent to "sync to one remote only."

Still good with this shape? If yes, I'd also like your call on the two open sub-questions from before: fail-closed when a configured `checkpoint_push_remote` names a nonexistent remote, and skip-sync on direct URL pushes (`git push git@github.com:...`).
if you never push the canonical remote, checkpoints accumulate locally and sync nowhere - isn't this the same as basically not pushing at all, which is expected then?

if you never push the canonical remote, checkpoints accumulate locally and sync nowhere - isn't this the same as basically not pushing at all, which is expected then? - or is this like if you never push to the highest remote it'll never get hte push? or like what does this eman

Good question — it's the second one, and it's a *new* kind of gap that can't happen today. Let me make it concrete.

**Today:** checkpoints piggyback on *every* push. Whatever remote you push, checkpoints ride along to it. So as long as you push *anywhere*, your checkpoints are backed up *somewhere*. The invariant is "code pushed ⇒ checkpoints pushed" — the bug is just that "somewhere" includes remotes like `publish` where you don't want them.

**After the fix:** checkpoints only ride along on pushes to the canonical remote. So consider this workflow:

```
remotes: origin (canonical), publish
you work, commit, and only ever run: git push publish
```

Your **code** is safely on `publish`. Your **checkpoints** are nowhere but your laptop — the `publish` pushes skip sync by design, and you never gave `origin` a push for them to ride on. If your disk dies, code survives, session history doesn't.

So it's *not* the same as "not pushing at all":

- **Never pushing at all** → nothing is remote, and you know it. Expected, no surprise.
- **Only pushing non-canonical remotes** → code is remote, checkpoints silently aren't. You *feel* backed up but half your data isn't. That's the surprising case.

To your "highest remote" phrasing — there's no ranking or cascade. It's binary: one remote is the checkpoint home; pushes to it sync checkpoints, pushes to anything else don't. Push it once a week and checkpoints catch up in that push (both backends accumulate unpushed state locally — the v1 branch just stays ahead of its remote-tracking ref, and the refs queue holds entries until a canonical push drains them). Nothing is lost, only deferred.

Worth saying: this asymmetry is *precisely what the ticket asks for*. Rizel doesn't want checkpoints on `publish`, so a `publish`-only pusher not syncing checkpoints is correct behavior, not a defect. The only design question is whether to leave the gap silent or nudge — e.g. `entire status` (or a rare pre-push hint) saying "12 checkpoints not yet synced — they push with `git push origin`." Given `status` already surfaces sync-ish state, a quiet status line feels right and a nagging hook message feels wrong.

Want me to include that status nudge in scope A, or keep the first PR to the pure resolver + gate?
"highest remote" - well then what did you mean by canonical

By "canonical remote" I just mean **the one remote the resolver elects as the checkpoint home** — nothing more. It's a label for the resolver's output, not a property remotes have or a hierarchy among them.

To git, all remotes are perfectly flat peers — `origin` isn't special in git's data model, there's no "primary" or "highest" remote anywhere. Git doesn't rank them; you push to whichever you name. So when this design needs *one* remote to carry checkpoints, someone has to pick it. The resolver is the picker, and its precedence list is the picking rule:

1. the remote you explicitly named in `checkpoint_push_remote`, if set
2. else `origin` (a *convention* — it's just the default name `git clone` assigns, which is also why every existing read path in the codebase guesses it)
3. else the only remote, if there's just one
4. else the first one listed in `.git/config`

Whichever rung matches, that single winner is what I've been calling "canonical." Maybe the clearer name is just **the checkpoint remote**: checkpoints sync when you push *it*, and never when you push anything else. There's no ranking where checkpoints "prefer" one remote but fall back to the next at push time — the precedence list runs once to elect a winner, and every other remote is simply excluded.

So in the earlier example: `origin` wins by rule 2, meaning `git push origin` syncs checkpoints and `git push publish` never does — not because origin outranks publish in some general sense, but because the resolver elected origin as the checkpoint home and publish lost by definition.

(And I'll use "checkpoint remote" going forward — "canonical" was jargon smuggled in from the design discussion, though note the settings knob can't be called `checkpoint_remote` since that name is already taken by the GitHub-coupled `{provider, repo}` feature.)
okay this makes sense, and so why is this a tradeoff then?

"Trade-off" only in the strict sense that we're exchanging one guarantee for another — not that it's a close call.

**What today's behavior gives you:** maximum durability by accident. Every push, to any remote, backs your checkpoints up somewhere. A user who only ever pushes `publish` still has their session history off-machine. Redundancy comes free — checkpoints might live on origin *and* publish *and* your backup mirror.

**What the fix gives you:** privacy and predictability. Checkpoints live exactly where you expect and nowhere else — never leaking transcripts onto a public or shared remote.

You can't have both, because they're answers to opposite questions — "spray everywhere so nothing is lost" versus "confine to one place so nothing leaks." Any design that syncs to exactly one remote necessarily gives up sync-on-every-push. That's the entire trade.

Why it's still clearly worth it:

- **The cost lands on almost nobody.** The typical repo has one remote, or has `origin` as the one that gets pushed constantly. For them the new behavior is byte-identical to today. The cost only exists in the corner case: multi-remote repos where the checkpoint remote is the one you *rarely or never* push.
- **The old guarantee was also the bug.** The "durability" of syncing everywhere is indistinguishable from the leak Rizel reported — they're the same mechanism. You can't keep the backup-everywhere property and fix ENT-1451.
- **Failure modes are asymmetric.** Deferred sync is recoverable — checkpoints sit locally until the next `git push origin`, then all catch up. A transcript pushed to `publish` is *not* recoverable: it's published, possibly fetched, possibly cached. When one failure mode is "later" and the other is "forever," you bias toward the recoverable one. (Same logic as fail-closed on a misconfigured knob.)

So I flagged it not because the decision is hard, but because it's a **silent behavior change**: someone with a rare workflow (publish-only pushing, or using a second remote as their checkpoint backup) loses something without an error message. Design reviews should name who gets hurt even when the answer is "very few people, and the changelog plus a status nudge covers them."

That closes the design discussion from my side. Still pending your call: fail-closed on a misconfigured `checkpoint_push_remote`, URL-push behavior, and whether the `entire status` nudge rides in this PR — then I can write up the plan.
well we should handle for cases where useres should be able to see where transcrips/checkpoints go for example and be able to recover this
Agreed — that turns the silent behavior change into an observable, recoverable one. Let me check what `entire status` and `entire doctor` already surface so the additions land in the right places.

The infrastructure for both halves already exists: `doctor` has a scan-and-fix flow with per-check confirmation (`confirmDoctorFix` in `doctor.go:409`), and `status` already renders per-session warnings and has a `--json` mode. Here's the visibility + recovery section of the design.

## Visibility: `entire status` tells you where checkpoints go

Two additions to `status` (text + `--json`):

1. **Destination line** — always shown when enabled: `Checkpoints sync to: origin` (annotated `(set by checkpoint_push_remote)` when configured, and a warning form when the configured remote doesn't exist — surfacing the fail-closed case instead of hiding it). JSON gets `checkpoint_remote` and `checkpoint_remote_source: "config" | "default" | "sole" | "first"`.
2. **Unpushed count** — `3 checkpoints not yet on origin — they sync with your next 'git push origin'`. Cheap and fully local: git-refs backend reads the push-queue length; git-branch compares local `entire/checkpoints/v1` against `refs/remotes/origin/entire/checkpoints/v1`. No network in `status`, matching its existing behavior. JSON: `unpushed_checkpoints: <n>`.

This closes the "silent gap" from the trade-off discussion: a publish-only pusher sees the counter grow and knows exactly which push drains it.

## Recovery: `entire doctor` finds and cleans up leaked checkpoints

A new doctor check alongside the existing ones (`checkDisconnectedMetadata` etc.), because Rizel's repo *already* has checkpoints on `publish` — the gate stops future leaks but doesn't undo past ones:

- **Detect:** for each configured remote that isn't the checkpoint remote, `ls-remote` for `entire/checkpoints/v1` and `refs/entire/*`. (Doctor may use the network, unlike the pre-push hot path; remote-tracking refs alone can be stale in both directions.)
- **Report:** `publish has checkpoint data (entire/checkpoints/v1, 47 refs) — checkpoints are configured to sync only to origin.`
- **Fix (confirmed via the existing prompt):** first verify the checkpoint remote has everything the stray remote has (fetch/compare), *then* `git push publish --delete` the branch and refs. Ordering matters — never delete the only copy. If origin is missing some, push them to origin first, then clean `publish`.
- **Honest caveat in the output:** deleting the ref removes it from the remote, but a forge may retain cached/forked copies — same disclosure git hosting docs give for removing sensitive data.

The same check covers the inverse recovery for free: if the *checkpoint* remote is missing locally-known checkpoints (the stranded-local case), doctor offers to push them directly rather than waiting for the next `git push origin`.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The split follows the repo's existing philosophy: `status` is the passive, no-network, always-cheap surface; `doctor` is the opt-in, network-allowed, scan-and-fix surface. Putting `ls-remote` in status would make every status call hang on a slow remote; putting recovery in status would bury a destructive action in a read command.
- "Verify-then-delete" is the same shape as the OPF pre-push rewrite's safety rules elsewhere in this codebase: never let a cleanup step be the operation that destroys the last copy.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## Updated scope A (final shape)

1. **PR core:** resolver (`checkpoint_push_remote` → `origin` → sole → first-in-config) + `prePush` gate, fail-closed on misconfigured name, URL-pushes skip sync. Fixes ENT-1451 + ENCLI-256.
2. **Visibility:** status destination line + unpushed counter (text + JSON).
3. **Recovery:** doctor check for checkpoint data on non-checkpoint remotes, verify-then-delete fix, plus push-missing-to-checkpoint-remote.

Probably 1 lands as its own PR and 2+3 as a fast-follow PR, so the behavior change ships small and reviewable. Unless you object, I'll take fail-closed and skip-on-URL-push as decided (both bias toward "don't leak"), and this is the design I'd write up. Approve, or anything else to fold in?

# Checkpoint Sync to a Single Remote — Design

**Date:** 2026-07-31
**Tickets:** ENT-1451 (primary), ENCLI-256 (fixed by construction), ENCLI-255 (follow-up enabled, not in scope)
**GitHub issues:** entireio/cli#1634, entireio/cli#1635

## Problem

In a repo with multiple remotes (e.g. `origin` and `publish`), a `git push` to
**any** remote syncs checkpoint data to that remote: the pre-push hook receives
the remote name as `$1` and `PrePush(ctx, remote)` follows it unconditionally.
Session transcripts therefore leak onto remotes where the user does not want
them (the reported case: a public `publish` remote).

Backend-specific shapes of the same defect:

- **git-branch primary:** every push re-syncs `entire/checkpoints/v1`, so every
  remote receives full transcripts (ENT-1451).
- **git-refs primary:** the flock-JSONL push queue (`checkpoint/pushqueue.go`)
  has no per-remote state; the first successful push drains it, so a second
  remote silently never receives per-checkpoint refs (ENCLI-256).

Additionally, all read/fetch paths hardcode `origin` (ENCLI-255), so pushes to
non-origin remotes strand checkpoints where reads never look.

## Goals

1. Checkpoint data syncs to exactly one remote — zero configuration in the
   common case.
2. Users can see where checkpoints go and how many are not yet synced.
3. Users can recover from past leaks (checkpoint data already on the wrong
   remote) and from stranded-local checkpoints.
4. Bias every ambiguous case toward "do not leak": a deferred sync is
   recoverable; a transcript pushed to a public remote is not.

## Non-goals

- Routing read/fetch paths through the new resolver (ENCLI-255). The resolver
  is built so that follow-up can reuse it, but read paths stay
  origin-hardcoded in this change. With the default resolution (`origin`
  wins), writes and reads agree in the common case.
- Multi-remote checkpoint replication (sync to N remotes). Explicitly
  unsupported after this change.
- Changes to the existing `checkpoint_remote` (`{provider, repo}`) feature.

## Design

### Unit 1: Checkpoint-remote resolver

`resolveCheckpointSyncRemote(ctx) (name string, source string, err error)` in
the `strategy` package (next to `resolvePushSettings` in
`checkpoint_remote.go`). Pure local lookup — no network. Precedence:

1. **`strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote`** (new setting; a plain git
   remote *name*, e.g. `"origin"` or `"private"`). If the named remote does
   not exist, resolution **fails closed**: the resolver returns an error, the
   pre-push gate skips checkpoint sync entirely, and `status` shows a warning.
   It must never silently fall back to another remote, because the user's
   explicit intent was to confine checkpoints to that remote.
2. **`origin`**, if configured (`git remote get-url origin` succeeds).
3. **The sole remote**, if exactly one is configured.
4. **The first remote in `.git/config` order** (config file section order
   approximates "first remote added"; `git remote` output is alphabetical and
   unsuitable). Read via `git config --get-regexp '^remote\..*\.url$'`, which
   preserves file order; take the first distinct remote name.
5. **No remotes configured:** resolver returns empty; the gate is a no-op
   (pre-push cannot fire without a remote anyway; status shows nothing).

`source` is one of `config | default | sole | first` for display and JSON.

Settings plumbing: new optional string field in
`settings/settings.go` under `strategy_options`, named
`checkpoint_push_remote`. Name is deliberately distinct from the existing
GitHub-coupled `checkpoint_remote` struct.

### Unit 2: Pre-push gate

In `strategy/manual_commit_push.go` `prePush(...)`, immediately after
`resolvePushSettings` and the existing `pushDisabled` early-return:

- **Exemption:** if `ps.hasCheckpointURL()` (a structured `checkpoint_remote`
  resolved to a dedicated URL), skip the gate. That feature routes checkpoint
  data to a dedicated store regardless of which remote triggered the push;
  its behavior is unchanged.
- **Gate:** resolve the checkpoint remote. If it differs from the hook's
  remote (`ps.remote`, git's `$1`), log a debug line
  (`checkpoint sync skipped: push remote %q is not the checkpoint remote %q`)
  and return nil. The user's push proceeds untouched: no v1 branch push, no
  per-checkpoint refs push, no queue drain, no OPF prompt, no
  checkpoint-policy sync side effects on that remote.
- **Resolver fail-closed / no-remote cases:** treat as non-matching — skip
  sync, log at warn (misconfigured name) or debug (no remotes).

Because the gate sits before both backend branches (the `PrimaryIsRefs`
dispatch and the git-branch path), it covers both backends:

- git-branch: non-checkpoint remotes never receive `entire/checkpoints/v1`.
- git-refs: only pushes to the checkpoint remote can drain the push queue, so
  "queue drained by the wrong remote" (ENCLI-256) becomes unrepresentable.
  This is ENCLI-256's "option 2" (delete only on push to the read-resolution
  target).

**URL pushes:** when the user runs `git push <url>` with a raw URL, git passes
the URL as `$1`. A URL never equals a configured remote name, so URL pushes
skip checkpoint sync. This is a deliberate behavior change (today they sync):
an ad-hoc URL push is even less the checkpoint home than a named secondary
remote. Pinned by a test.

### Unit 3: Status visibility

`entire status` (text and `--json`), always shown when Entire is enabled and
at least one remote exists:

1. **Destination line:** `Checkpoints sync to: origin`, annotated
   `(set by checkpoint_push_remote)` when source is `config`. When the
   configured name does not resolve:
   `Checkpoints NOT syncing: checkpoint_push_remote "private" is not a
   configured remote`. JSON fields: `checkpoint_remote` (string, empty when
   unresolved), `checkpoint_remote_source` (`config|default|sole|first`),
   plus the existing error surfaces for the misconfigured case.
2. **Unpushed counter:** `N checkpoints not yet on origin — they sync with
   your next 'git push origin'`. Computed fully locally (status makes no
   network calls): git-refs backend reads the push-queue length; git-branch
   compares local `entire/checkpoints/v1` against
   `refs/remotes/<checkpoint-remote>/entire/checkpoints/v1` (commit count
   ahead; absent tracking ref with a local v1 branch counts as "all
   unpushed"). Omitted when the count is 0. JSON field:
   `unpushed_checkpoints` (int).

The counter closes the observability gap created by the gate: a user who only
pushes non-checkpoint remotes sees the number grow and knows exactly which
push drains it.

### Unit 4: Doctor recovery

A new check in the `entire doctor` scan-and-fix flow (alongside
`checkDisconnectedMetadata` etc.), using the existing `confirmDoctorFix`
confirmation pattern. Doctor may use the network (unlike status and the
pre-push hot path).

**Detect:** for each configured remote other than the checkpoint remote,
`ls-remote` for `refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1` and `refs/entire/*`.
Remote-tracking refs alone are not trusted (stale in both directions).

**Report:** e.g. `publish has checkpoint data (entire/checkpoints/v1, 47
per-checkpoint refs) — checkpoints are configured to sync only to origin.`

**Fix (per remote, after confirmation), verify-then-delete:**

1. Ensure the checkpoint remote has every object the stray remote has:
   fetch the stray remote's checkpoint refs, compare, and push anything
   missing to the checkpoint remote first. Never delete the only copy.
2. Then delete from the stray remote: `git push <remote> --delete
   entire/checkpoints/v1` and `git push <remote> ':refs/entire/*'` (refspec
   deletes for the refs backend).
3. Output an honest caveat: deleting refs removes them from the remote, but a
   forge may retain cached, forked, or archived copies — same disclosure git
   hosting providers give for sensitive-data removal.

**Inverse recovery (same check):** if the checkpoint remote is missing
locally-known checkpoints (stranded-local case), doctor offers to push them
directly instead of waiting for the user's next `git push <checkpoint
remote>`.

Failure handling: each remote is processed independently; an unreachable
remote reports and skips (does not abort the doctor run). Deletion is only
attempted after step 1 succeeds for that remote.

## Behavior change and who it affects

This changes a default. Today, checkpoints piggyback on every push, so
pushing anywhere backs them up somewhere (and leaks them everywhere). After
this change they sync only to the checkpoint remote.

- Single-remote repos and repos where `origin` is the routinely pushed
  remote: behavior identical to today.
- Multi-remote repos where the user relies on a secondary remote receiving
  checkpoints (e.g. as backup): they lose that silently at push time.
  Mitigations: the status destination line + unpushed counter, the debug log
  in the hook, a changelog entry, and `checkpoint_push_remote` as the escape
  hatch for choosing *which* remote (multi-remote replication is explicitly
  out).

## Testing

- **Unit (strategy):** resolver precedence table — override set (valid and
  fail-closed invalid), origin present, sole remote, origin-less multi-remote
  first-in-config order, no remotes. Gate behavior with mocked settings.
- **Integration (`cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/`, isolated temp repos per
  CLAUDE.md):** two local bare remotes `origin` + `publish`; for **both
  backends**: push `publish` → no checkpoint refs / no v1 branch there, refs
  queue intact; then push `origin` → checkpoints land, queue drained.
  Variants: `checkpoint_push_remote` selecting the non-origin remote;
  misconfigured name (fail-closed: neither remote receives checkpoints); raw
  URL push (skips sync); `checkpoint_remote` URL configured (gate exempt).
  Status: destination line, source annotation, unpushed counter before/after
  push, `--json` fields. Doctor: seeded stray checkpoints on `publish` →
  detect, verify-then-delete, stray remote missing from checkpoint remote →
  pushed before delete; unreachable remote skipped.
- **Interaction with PR stack #1637–#1639:**
  `TestGitRefsQueue_TwoRemotesQueueClearedByFirstPush` (#1638) pins today's
  ENCLI-256 behavior with a flip-me comment. If the stack merges first, this
  change flips that assertion; otherwise this change ships its own equivalent
  test and the stack rebases.
- Standard repo gate before commit: `mise run check`.

## Delivery

Two PRs:

1. **Core:** resolver + settings field + pre-push gate + unit/integration
   tests + changelog note. Fixes ENT-1451 and ENCLI-256.
2. **Fast-follow:** status visibility + doctor recovery.

Follow-up (separate design): route read/fetch paths through the resolver
(ENCLI-255), unblocking the B1–B7 tests of
`docs/testing/git-remote-test-plan.md` (decision D-1 resolves as
"single checkpoint remote, default origin").

Let me take the three questions one at a time.

**1. Do checkpoints push to both today?** Depends on the backend, and it's messier than "both":

- **git-branch backend:** each push syncs the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch *to the remote you're pushing*. So push `origin` → checkpoints on origin; push `publish` → checkpoints on publish too. Push both regularly and yes, both have them. This is Rizel's complaint.
- **git-refs backend:** neither reliably! The push queue is drained by whichever push happens *first*. Push `origin` then `publish` → origin has the checkpoints, publish permanently misses them (ENCLI-256). It's not "both", it's "whoever pushed first, at random from the user's perspective."

So today's behavior isn't a coherent "sync to all remotes" feature — it's undefined behavior falling out of the hook mechanics, that happens to look like "all remotes" on one backend and "random single remote" on the other.

**2. Should the user be able to choose one, or multiple?** Choosing **which one** — yes, that's in the design: `checkpoint_push_remote: "private"` picks any remote, and the zero-config default is origin. Choosing **multiple** — the design deliberately says no, and here's the reasoning:

- Nobody has asked for it. The one real user signal (ENT-1451) asks for *fewer* remotes, not a fan-out feature. Classic YAGNI.
- Multi-remote sync is a genuinely harder feature, not just a longer list: the git-refs queue would need per-remote tracking (entries removed only when *every* target has the ref — ENCLI-256's "option 1", the complex fix we avoided), and reads would need an ordering story (which remote does resume/explain fetch from when they disagree?).
- It's **not foreclosed**. The setting is a single string today; if a real request for replication shows up, it can grow into a list (`checkpoint_push_remotes: [...]`) and the gate becomes a set-membership check. The expensive part (per-remote queue state) only gets built when someone actually wants it.

If you think replication is a likely near-term ask, I can add a "future evolution" note to the spec so the follow-up doesn't fight the design — but I wouldn't put it in scope.

**3. Was the test stack allowing or guarding?** Neither — it's deliberately opinion-free. The stack pins *whatever the code does today* (including the git-refs "first push wins" bug, with a comment saying "flip me when fixed") and explicitly punted the should-question to decision D-1 in the test plan, which the author left undecided. It doesn't enable multi-remote sync, doesn't prevent it, and doesn't protect it — it just makes today's accidental behavior visible in executable form so that whichever answer got chosen (our spec is that answer) shows up in review as consciously flipped assertions rather than silent semantic drift.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- "One remote, choosable, extensible-to-many-later" is the classic way to sequence this: the single-string knob delivers the user's actual need now, while a list-shaped future stays cheap because the gate logic (`is this push's remote in the allowed set?`) is shape-agnostic. What *would* be expensive later — per-remote queue bookkeeping — is exactly the part no one has requested.
- The backend asymmetry in question 1 is the strongest argument that today's "both remotes" was never a feature: a feature would behave the same on both backends. Accidental behavior can't be "kept" — there's nothing coherent to keep.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Want me to add the future-evolution note (single string → list) to the spec, or leave it as-is?

The backend mess I described in question 1 is precisely what dies with this change — "both remotes" (git-branch) and "first push wins" (git-refs) both collapse into the same rule. Split — but I'd re-draw the seam rather than just cutting PR 2 in half, ending with two PRs total, differently shaped:

**PR 1: gate + resolver + status visibility.** My earlier split put visibility in the follow-up, but that's backwards: the status line and unpushed counter are the *mitigation* for PR 1's silent behavior change. A user whose checkpoints stop landing on `publish` should get the "checkpoints sync to origin / N not yet pushed" signal in the same release the behavior changes, not one release later. The visibility code is also mostly plumbing (~80–100 lines of the resolver's output into two render paths) that reviews in minutes and shares the resolver's test fixtures. Adding it keeps PR 1 at roughly 350–450 production lines — still one sitting.

**PR 2: doctor recovery alone.** This is the piece that genuinely deserves its own PR, for reasons beyond size:

- **It deletes refs from users' remotes.** That's the highest-consequence code in the whole design, and it deserves a review where it's the *only* thing on screen — the verify-then-delete ordering, the never-delete-the-last-copy invariant, the per-remote error isolation. Mixing it with status plumbing invites reviewer attention to spread exactly where it shouldn't.
- **Different failure blast radius.** A bug in PR 1 means checkpoints sync to the wrong place or defer — recoverable. A bug in PR 2's deletion path is permanent data loss. Different risk classes shouldn't share a merge decision; if review turns up something in the deletion logic, that shouldn't hold the leak fix hostage.
- **No urgency coupling.** The gate stops *future* leaks the day it ships. Cleaning up *past* leaks is important but not time-sensitive — the stray data on `publish` has been there for months; a week between PRs changes nothing.
- **It's independently testable and revertable** — a self-contained new doctor check touching none of PR 1's files except reading the resolver.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** This should be run in a dedicated worktree (created by brainstorming skill).

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Bite-Sized Task Granularity

**Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step

```go
// resolveMigratePushRemote picks the remote migrated refs push to: the
// explicit --remote value if given, else the elected checkpoint sync
// remote. Fail-closed (spec: non-hook drain paths): a misconfigured
// checkpoint_push_remote is an error, never a fallback to origin.
func resolveMigratePushRemote(ctx context.Context, explicit string) (string, error) {
	if explicit != "" {
		return explicit, nil
	}
	syncRemote, err := strategy.ResolveCheckpointSyncRemote(ctx)
	if err != nil {
		return "", fmt.Errorf("cannot determine checkpoint sync remote (pass --remote explicitly): %w", err)
	}
	if syncRemote.Name == "" {
		return "", fmt.Errorf("no git remotes configured; pass --remote explicitly")
	}
	return syncRemote.Name, nil
}
```

the `confirmDoctorFix` prompt at ~line 85 (never after — a resolution error

```go
	if err != nil {

	}
```

# Using Git Worktrees

## Overview

Git worktrees create isolated workspaces sharing the same repository, allowing work on multiple branches simultaneously without switching.

**Core principle:** Systematic directory selection + safety verification = reliable isolation.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the using-git-worktrees skill to set up an isolated workspace."

## Directory Selection Process

Follow this priority order:

### 1. Check Existing Directories

```bash
# Check in priority order
ls -d .worktrees 2>/dev/null     # Preferred (hidden)
ls -d worktrees 2>/dev/null      # Alternative
```

**If found:** Use that directory. If both exist, `.worktrees` wins.

### 2. Check CLAUDE.md

```bash
grep -i "worktree.*director" CLAUDE.md 2>/dev/null
```

**If preference specified:** Use it without asking.

### 3. Ask User

If no directory exists and no CLAUDE.md preference:

```
No worktree directory found. Where should I create worktrees?

1. .worktrees/ (project-local, hidden)
2. ~/.config/superpowers/worktrees/<project-name>/ (global location)

Which would you prefer?
```

## Safety Verification

### For Project-Local Directories (.worktrees or worktrees)

**MUST verify directory is ignored before creating worktree:**

```bash
# Check if directory is ignored (respects local, global, and system gitignore)
git check-ignore -q .worktrees 2>/dev/null || git check-ignore -q worktrees 2>/dev/null
```

**If NOT ignored:**

Per Jesse's rule "Fix broken things immediately":
1. Add appropriate line to .gitignore
2. Commit the change
3. Proceed with worktree creation

**Why critical:** Prevents accidentally committing worktree contents to repository.

### For Global Directory (~/.config/superpowers/worktrees)

No .gitignore verification needed - outside project entirely.

## Creation Steps

### 1. Detect Project Name

```bash
project=$(basename "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)")
```

### 2. Create Worktree

```bash
# Determine full path
case $LOCATION in
  .worktrees|worktrees)
    path="$LOCATION/$BRANCH_NAME"
    ;;
  ~/.config/superpowers/worktrees/*)
    path="~/.config/superpowers/worktrees/$project/$BRANCH_NAME"
    ;;
esac

# Create worktree with new branch
git worktree add "$path" -b "$BRANCH_NAME"
cd "$path"
```

### 3. Run Project Setup

Auto-detect and run appropriate setup:

```bash
# Node.js
if [ -f package.json ]; then npm install; fi

# Rust
if [ -f Cargo.toml ]; then cargo build; fi

# Python
if [ -f requirements.txt ]; then pip install -r requirements.txt; fi
if [ -f pyproject.toml ]; then poetry install; fi

# Go
if [ -f go.mod ]; then go mod download; fi
```

### 4. Verify Clean Baseline

Run tests to ensure worktree starts clean:

```bash
# Examples - use project-appropriate command
npm test
cargo test
pytest
go test ./...
```

**If tests fail:** Report failures, ask whether to proceed or investigate.

**If tests pass:** Report ready.

### 5. Report Location

```
Worktree ready at <full-path>
Tests passing (<N> tests, 0 failures)
Ready to implement <feature-name>
```

## Quick Reference

| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| `.worktrees/` exists | Use it (verify ignored) |
| `worktrees/` exists | Use it (verify ignored) |
| Both exist | Use `.worktrees/` |
| Neither exists | Check CLAUDE.md → Ask user |
| Directory not ignored | Add to .gitignore + commit |
| Tests fail during baseline | Report failures + ask |
| No package.json/Cargo.toml | Skip dependency install |

## Common Mistakes

### Skipping ignore verification

- **Problem:** Worktree contents get tracked, pollute git status
- **Fix:** Always use `git check-ignore` before creating project-local worktree

### Assuming directory location

- **Problem:** Creates inconsistency, violates project conventions
- **Fix:** Follow priority: existing > CLAUDE.md > ask

### Proceeding with failing tests

- **Problem:** Can't distinguish new bugs from pre-existing issues
- **Fix:** Report failures, get explicit permission to proceed

### Hardcoding setup commands

- **Problem:** Breaks on projects using different tools
- **Fix:** Auto-detect from project files (package.json, etc.)

## Example Workflow

```
You: I'm using the using-git-worktrees skill to set up an isolated workspace.

[Check .worktrees/ - exists]
[Verify ignored - git check-ignore confirms .worktrees/ is ignored]
[Create worktree: git worktree add .worktrees/auth -b feature/auth]
[Run npm install]
[Run npm test - 47 passing]

Worktree ready at /Users/jesse/myproject/.worktrees/auth
Tests passing (47 tests, 0 failures)
Ready to implement auth feature
```

## Red Flags

**Never:**
- Create worktree without verifying it's ignored (project-local)
- Skip baseline test verification
- Proceed with failing tests without asking
- Assume directory location when ambiguous
- Skip CLAUDE.md check

**Always:**
- Follow directory priority: existing > CLAUDE.md > ask
- Verify directory is ignored for project-local
- Auto-detect and run project setup
- Verify clean test baseline

## Integration

**Called by:**
- **brainstorming** (Phase 4) - REQUIRED when design is approved and implementation follows
- **subagent-driven-development** - REQUIRED before executing any tasks
- **executing-plans** - REQUIRED before executing any tasks
- Any skill needing isolated workspace

**Pairs with:**
- **finishing-a-development-branch** - REQUIRED for cleanup after work complete

# Subagent-Driven Development

Execute plan by dispatching fresh subagent per task, with two-stage review after each: spec compliance review first, then code quality review.

**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.

**Core principle:** Fresh subagent per task + two-stage review (spec then quality) = high quality, fast iteration

## When to Use

```dot
digraph when_to_use {
    "Have implementation plan?" [shape=diamond];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" [shape=diamond];
    "Stay in this session?" [shape=diamond];
    "subagent-driven-development" [shape=box];
    "executing-plans" [shape=box];
    "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [shape=box];

    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Tasks mostly independent?" [label="yes"];
    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no"];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Stay in this session?" [label="yes"];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no - tightly coupled"];
    "Stay in this session?" -> "subagent-driven-development" [label="yes"];
    "Stay in this session?" -> "executing-plans" [label="no - parallel session"];
}
```

**vs. Executing Plans (parallel session):**
- Same session (no context switch)
- Fresh subagent per task (no context pollution)
- Two-stage review after each task: spec compliance first, then code quality
- Faster iteration (no human-in-loop between tasks)

## The Process

```dot
digraph process {
    rankdir=TB;

    subgraph cluster_per_task {
        label="Per Task";
        "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)" [shape=box];
        "Implementer subagent asks questions?" [shape=diamond];
        "Answer questions, provide context" [shape=box];
        "Implementer subagent implements, tests, commits, self-reviews" [shape=box];
        "Dispatch spec reviewer subagent (./spec-reviewer-prompt.md)" [shape=box];
        "Spec reviewer subagent confirms code matches spec?" [shape=diamond];
        "Implementer subagent fixes spec gaps" [shape=box];
        "Dispatch code quality reviewer subagent (./code-quality-reviewer-prompt.md)" [shape=box];
        "Code quality reviewer subagent approves?" [shape=diamond];
        "Implementer subagent fixes quality issues" [shape=box];
        "Mark task complete in TodoWrite" [shape=box];
    }

    "Read plan, extract all tasks with full text, note context, create TodoWrite" [shape=box];
    "More tasks remain?" [shape=diamond];
    "Dispatch final code reviewer subagent for entire implementation" [shape=box];
    "Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch" [shape=box style=filled fillcolor=lightgreen];

    "Read plan, extract all tasks with full text, note context, create TodoWrite" -> "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)";
    "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)" -> "Implementer subagent asks questions?";
    "Implementer subagent asks questions?" -> "Answer questions, provide context" [label="yes"];
    "Answer questions, provide context" -> "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)";
    "Implementer subagent asks questions?" -> "Implementer subagent implements, tests, commits, self-reviews" [label="no"];
    "Implementer subagent implements, tests, commits, self-reviews" -> "Dispatch spec reviewer subagent (./spec-reviewer-prompt.md)";
    "Dispatch spec reviewer subagent (./spec-reviewer-prompt.md)" -> "Spec reviewer subagent confirms code matches spec?";
    "Spec reviewer subagent confirms code matches spec?" -> "Implementer subagent fixes spec gaps" [label="no"];
    "Implementer subagent fixes spec gaps" -> "Dispatch spec reviewer subagent (./spec-reviewer-prompt.md)" [label="re-review"];
    "Spec reviewer subagent confirms code matches spec?" -> "Dispatch code quality reviewer subagent (./code-quality-reviewer-prompt.md)" [label="yes"];
    "Dispatch code quality reviewer subagent (./code-quality-reviewer-prompt.md)" -> "Code quality reviewer subagent approves?";
    "Code quality reviewer subagent approves?" -> "Implementer subagent fixes quality issues" [label="no"];
    "Implementer subagent fixes quality issues" -> "Dispatch code quality reviewer subagent (./code-quality-reviewer-prompt.md)" [label="re-review"];
    "Code quality reviewer subagent approves?" -> "Mark task complete in TodoWrite" [label="yes"];
    "Mark task complete in TodoWrite" -> "More tasks remain?";
    "More tasks remain?" -> "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)" [label="yes"];
    "More tasks remain?" -> "Dispatch final code reviewer subagent for entire implementation" [label="no"];
    "Dispatch final code reviewer subagent for entire implementation" -> "Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch";
}
```

## Model Selection

Use the least powerful model that can handle each role to conserve cost and increase speed.

**Mechanical implementation tasks** (isolated functions, clear specs, 1-2 files): use a fast, cheap model. Most implementation tasks are mechanical when the plan is well-specified.

**Integration and judgment tasks** (multi-file coordination, pattern matching, debugging): use a standard model.

**Architecture, design, and review tasks**: use the most capable available model.

**Task complexity signals:**
- Touches 1-2 files with a complete spec → cheap model
- Touches multiple files with integration concerns → standard model
- Requires design judgment or broad codebase understanding → most capable model

## Handling Implementer Status

Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:

**DONE:** Proceed to spec compliance review.

**DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review.

**NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch.

**BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker:
1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model
2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model
3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces
4. If the plan itself is wrong, escalate to the human

**Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change.

## Prompt Templates

- `./implementer-prompt.md` - Dispatch implementer subagent
- `./spec-reviewer-prompt.md` - Dispatch spec compliance reviewer subagent
- `./code-quality-reviewer-prompt.md` - Dispatch code quality reviewer subagent

## Example Workflow

```
You: I'm using Subagent-Driven Development to execute this plan.

[Read plan file once: docs/superpowers/plans/feature-plan.md]
[Extract all 5 tasks with full text and context]
[Create TodoWrite with all tasks]

Task 1: Hook installation script

[Get Task 1 text and context (already extracted)]
[Dispatch implementation subagent with full task text + context]

Implementer: "Before I begin - should the hook be installed at user or system level?"

You: "User level (~/.config/superpowers/hooks/)"

Implementer: "Got it. Implementing now..."
[Later] Implementer:
  - Implemented install-hook command
  - Added tests, 5/5 passing
  - Self-review: Found I missed --force flag, added it
  - Committed

[Dispatch spec compliance reviewer]
Spec reviewer: ✅ Spec compliant - all requirements met, nothing extra

[Get git SHAs, dispatch code quality reviewer]
Code reviewer: Strengths: Good test coverage, clean. Issues: None. Approved.

[Mark Task 1 complete]

Task 2: Recovery modes

[Get Task 2 text and context (already extracted)]
[Dispatch implementation subagent with full task text + context]

Implementer: [No questions, proceeds]
Implementer:
  - Added verify/repair modes
  - 8/8 tests passing
  - Self-review: All good
  - Committed

[Dispatch spec compliance reviewer]
Spec reviewer: ❌ Issues:
  - Missing: Progress reporting (spec says "report every 100 items")
  - Extra: Added --json flag (not requested)

[Implementer fixes issues]
Implementer: Removed --json flag, added progress reporting

[Spec reviewer reviews again]
Spec reviewer: ✅ Spec compliant now

[Dispatch code quality reviewer]
Code reviewer: Strengths: Solid. Issues (Important): Magic number (100)

[Implementer fixes]
Implementer: Extracted PROGRESS_INTERVAL constant

[Code reviewer reviews again]
Code reviewer: ✅ Approved

[Mark Task 2 complete]

...

[After all tasks]
[Dispatch final code-reviewer]
Final reviewer: All requirements met, ready to merge

Done!
```

## Advantages

**vs. Manual execution:**
- Subagents follow TDD naturally
- Fresh context per task (no confusion)
- Parallel-safe (subagents don't interfere)
- Subagent can ask questions (before AND during work)

**vs. Executing Plans:**
- Same session (no handoff)
- Continuous progress (no waiting)
- Review checkpoints automatic

**Efficiency gains:**
- No file reading overhead (controller provides full text)
- Controller curates exactly what context is needed
- Subagent gets complete information upfront
- Questions surfaced before work begins (not after)

**Quality gates:**
- Self-review catches issues before handoff
- Two-stage review: spec compliance, then code quality
- Review loops ensure fixes actually work
- Spec compliance prevents over/under-building
- Code quality ensures implementation is well-built

**Cost:**
- More subagent invocations (implementer + 2 reviewers per task)
- Controller does more prep work (extracting all tasks upfront)
- Review loops add iterations
- But catches issues early (cheaper than debugging later)

## Red Flags

**Never:**
- Start implementation on main/master branch without explicit user consent
- Skip reviews (spec compliance OR code quality)
- Proceed with unfixed issues
- Dispatch multiple implementation subagents in parallel (conflicts)
- Make subagent read plan file (provide full text instead)
- Skip scene-setting context (subagent needs to understand where task fits)
- Ignore subagent questions (answer before letting them proceed)
- Accept "close enough" on spec compliance (spec reviewer found issues = not done)
- Skip review loops (reviewer found issues = implementer fixes = review again)
- Let implementer self-review replace actual review (both are needed)
- **Start code quality review before spec compliance is ✅** (wrong order)
- Move to next task while either review has open issues

**If subagent asks questions:**
- Answer clearly and completely
- Provide additional context if needed
- Don't rush them into implementation

**If reviewer finds issues:**
- Implementer (same subagent) fixes them
- Reviewer reviews again
- Repeat until approved
- Don't skip the re-review

**If subagent fails task:**
- Dispatch fix subagent with specific instructions
- Don't try to fix manually (context pollution)

## Integration

**Required workflow skills:**
- **superpowers:using-git-worktrees** - REQUIRED: Set up isolated workspace before starting
- **superpowers:writing-plans** - Creates the plan this skill executes
- **superpowers:requesting-code-review** - Code review template for reviewer subagents
- **superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch** - Complete development after all tasks

**Subagents should use:**
- **superpowers:test-driven-development** - Subagents follow TDD for each task

**Alternative workflow:**
- **superpowers:executing-plans** - Use for parallel session instead of same-session execution
